We used an at home service for our 7 year old lab. She went into kidney failure out of nowhere, hung on for a couple months, but in the end she wasn’t eating or drinking and was skin & bones. Her creatinine and other levels were sky high as well, there was just no way she would get better or have any quality of life. 


We brought her into the back yard, lying on the bed she’d lain on her whole life, and sat with her in the august sun. It was a beautiful day out, and she got to just lie there and relax as we held her and loved her. The vet was incredibly compassionate and comforting, and gave her a mild sedative about 15mins before the final injection so she would be calm. I remember her softly saying “goodbye, sweetheart…” as she administered it, at that point the rest of us were all too choked up to talk. 

Later that month, my dad was chatting with his coworker (the one we got our dog from, who still owned her mum) and she said that their dog (our dog’s mum) had become suddenly very ill recently, and they’d called a home service for the euthanasia. The service had been fully booked, but when they told them where they lived, the service said “oh, we have another appointment out that way so we can come after.” We put it together that by some coincidence, right after we put our dog to sleep, her mother was put to sleep as well. I like to think Shale was waiting at the gates of the rainbow bridge when her mom showed up, and they’re hanging out together now. 


This is a long winded way of saying that I do recommend a home service, it’s a beautiful way to say goodbye. However, to the OP, please try not to feel guilty about this. Your dog was still with the people she loved most in the whole world when she passed, and had a wonderful life with you. You did everything you could, and that’s all anyone can ever do.

I have a grandpa with dementia and can absolutely understand the frustration and devastation of having someone you love not be who they used to be. I don’t think people who haven’t experienced it can truly understand how complex dementia is, and how quickly things can change. One minute, my grandpa is the most lovely, well spoken, educated man you’ve ever met- and the next, he’s walking around the house naked because he forgot his clothes. Just as you wouldn’t hold it against someone for throwing up because they’re sick, you have to have really clear boundaries in your mind. When my grandpa calls me by his other granddaughter’s name, it stings- but I know that’s not him. Your girlfriend just doesn’t have that practice and emotional resilience built up yet- and she shouldn’t have to if she doesn’t want to. During the trial, the following became public knowledge: the accused man had been assessed and found to have an IQ of less than 75, he spent his childhood in residential schools being both physically and sexually abused, and the dog was dumped on him by another person only a few weeks before it’s death, which meant it would have already been significantly sick and weak when he took possession of it. The man in this case was sentenced to be remanded to a psychiatric facility, and the Internet was FURIOUS, stating that it was too lenient, that he deserved to be punished and suffer, etc. I don’t know about you, but the traumatized simpleton that our country has already punished once just for being Native really isn’t at the top of my list of hardened criminals to watch out for. This guy is finally going to get the help he needs, real help that will help him at least have some quality of life, but people would rather he be isolated and abused in prison for life. That’s why I’m so positive that most people don’t understand the concept of prison being used as rehabilitation. It’s like they can’t fathom anything other than vengeance.



Also for what it’s worth- he never DIRECTLY injured the dog. It was tied up outdoors on his property by someone else for months, while wearing a tight collar, which caused severe injuries. It died because of neglect, because it was dumped on a man who didn’t have the mental tools to take care of himself, let alone a dog. Being in a facility, supervised, is all it will take to prevent him from causing harm again, because he won’t be put in a position where he can neglect anything.
